_comment: Mutations for the two background-loop bodies. Scored against loops_run.sh, the probe pair — no HTTP harness can reach either one. This spec matters more than most: the plan names these loops as "the least testable part and the most likely to silently diverge, because nothing calls them and nothing returns", and the Python's own history bears that out — an AttributeError in the cleanup ran nightly, swallowed by the loop's try/except, until a Sentry alert surfaced it. Several mutations here change a COUNT and nothing else, or the rows and not the count; the probe prints both for that reason. Extended to the five bodies the first pass did not cover — the reaper, the motion digest, the licence check-in, the plan reconcile and the data sync — plus the disk check, which has no HTTP surface at all. Several are marked equivalent with the reason: a concurrent write landing between a SELECT and an UPDATE is not something a single-threaded probe can arrange, and saying so is better than leaving the predicate looking untested.

mutations.name: a node never heard from is announced as offline
mutations._why: `last_seen IS NOT NULL` is the filter that keeps a row which has never reported from being announced as having gone offline. Drop it and every freshly created node gets a spurious 'went offline' the first time the sweep runs — before its first heartbeat, which is exactly the window an operator is watching.
mutations.old:
"UPDATE camera_nodes SET status = 'offline', updated_at = $2
          WHERE status = 'online' AND last_seen IS NOT NULL AND last_seen < $1
mutations.new:
"UPDATE camera_nodes SET status = 'offline', updated_at = $2
          WHERE status = 'online' AND last_seen < $1
mutations.equivalent: Equivalent, and verified rather than assumed: `NULL < timestamp` evaluates to NULL and `WHERE` treats that as not-true, so the comparison ALONE already excludes a row that has never reported. Checked against the fixture — 2 rows matched with the predicate and 2 without. SQLAlchemy emits the same SQL, so it is equally redundant in the Python. The predicate stays in both because it states the intent, and this entry stays so the next reader does not take its presence for evidence that it is load-bearing.

mutations.name: a camera never heard from is announced as offline
mutations._why: The same filter on the camera half. Separate mutation because it is a separate statement and a port can easily carry one and not the other.
mutations.old: WHERE c.status = 'online' AND c.last_seen IS NOT NULL AND c.last_seen < $1
mutations.equivalent: Equivalent, and verified rather than assumed: `NULL < timestamp` evaluates to NULL and `WHERE` treats that as not-true, so the comparison ALONE already excludes a row that has never reported. Checked against the fixture — 2 rows matched with the predicate and 2 without. SQLAlchemy emits the same SQL, so it is equally redundant in the Python. The predicate stays in both because it states the intent, and this entry stays so the next reader does not take its presence for evidence that it is load-bearing.

mutations.name: an already-offline node is announced again
mutations._why: `status = 'online'` is what makes the sweep a TRANSITION and not a state assertion. Without it every stale row is re-announced on every tick — one notification per node every thirty seconds, forever.
mutations.old: WHERE status = 'online' AND last_seen IS NOT NULL AND last_seen < $1
mutations.new: WHERE last_seen IS NOT NULL AND last_seen < $1

mutations.name: the heartbeat threshold is ten times too long
mutations._why: 90 seconds, and it has to be the same 90 `effective_status` uses — at 900 a camera reads offline in the dashboard for a quarter of an hour while the sweep still thinks it is online, so no notification ever fires for it.

mutations.name: a nameless node is announced with an empty title
mutations._why: `name or node_id` — a node whose name is blank is announced by its id, because a notification reading "Node '' went offline" tells an operator nothing about which box to go and look at.

mutations.name: a camera's transition loses its parent node
mutations._why: The notification's `node_id` is how the dashboard groups a camera's alert under the box that hosts it. Resolved through the FK rather than assumed, because a camera may have no node at all.
mutations.old: (SELECT n.node_id FROM camera_nodes n WHERE n.id = c.node_id) AS parent",

mutations.name: cameras are announced before nodes
mutations._why: Nodes first, then cameras — the notification ids follow the emit order and a client renders the inbox by id, so an operator sees the uplink drop before the cameras behind it rather than after. Invisible to a snapshot that sorts by anything but id, which is why the probe carries a row_number.

mutations.name: every org gets the same retention
mutations._why: Retention is the tier's, not a constant: Free 30 days, Pro 90, Pro Plus 365. A fixed 90 silently deletes eleven months of a Pro Plus org's audit trail and keeps two months of a free one's.

mutations.name: notifications are swept on the wrong column
mutations._why: `notifications` is the one log table whose timestamp is `created_at`; three others use `timestamp` and the stream log uses `accessed_at`. They are not interchangeable — and a wrong guess here does not error, it deletes nothing and reports zero, which reads exactly like a clean sweep.
mutations.old: "DELETE FROM notifications WHERE org_id = $1 AND created_at < $2",
mutations.new: "DELETE FROM notifications WHERE org_id = $1 AND created_at < $2 AND false",

mutations.name: a pending email is deleted with the old sent ones
mutations._why: The outbox sweep is terminal-state only. A pending or sending row is an email that has NOT gone out yet, and deleting one loses it with nothing left to show it existed — the fixture carries a 400-day pending row for exactly this.

mutations.name: the outbox window follows the tier
mutations._why: Seven days, fixed and cross-org. The outbox is a queue the worker scans every tick, so it wants to be small at all times; the long-term per-org trail is email_log's job. A 365-day window on a Pro Plus org makes the hot scan target a year deep.

mutations.name: webhook markers are swept inside Svix's retry window
mutations._why: 30 days, chosen to comfortably exceed Svix's ~5-day retry window. Sweep at 3 and a retried delivery finds no marker and double-processes — which for a subscription webhook means re-applying a plan change, and for Resend means re-suppressing an address.

mutations.name: an org with only email activity is skipped
mutations._why: `email_log` is in the UNION so an org whose only rows are emails still has its retention applied. Without it that org's log grows forever, and it is the least likely to be noticed because nothing else about the org looks active. Scored zero until the fixture gained `loops-email`, an org with rows in email_log and nowhere else: every other org here has rows in all six tables, so dropping that UNION arm changed the org set not at all.

mutations.name: an empty org_id is swept as an org
mutations._why: Python filters on `if row[0]`, which is false for an empty string as well as NULL. An empty org_id is a corrupt row; resolving a plan for it means a Clerk lookup for an org that does not exist, and counting it inflates orgs_processed. Scored zero until the fixture gained an audit_log row with an EMPTY org_id — there was nothing for the filter to filter.

mutations.name: the org list counts duplicates
mutations._why: UNION, not UNION ALL: an org with rows in all six tables appears six times under ALL, which sweeps it six times (harmless, the second is a no-op) and reports orgs_processed six times too high — the one number an operator uses to sanity-check the sweep. EVERY union has to change: the first version of this mutation changed only the first, and `A UNION ALL B UNION C` still dedupes the whole accumulated result at the later UNION, so the mutant was equivalent by construction.
mutations.old:
"SELECT org_id FROM stream_access_logs
         UNION SELECT org_id FROM mcp_activity_logs
         UNION SELECT org_id FROM audit_log
         UNION SELECT org_id FROM motion_events
         UNION SELECT org_id FROM notifications
         UNION SELECT org_id FROM email_log",
mutations.new:
"SELECT org_id FROM stream_access_logs
         UNION ALL SELECT org_id FROM mcp_activity_logs
         UNION ALL SELECT org_id FROM audit_log
         UNION ALL SELECT org_id FROM motion_events
         UNION ALL SELECT org_id FROM notifications
         UNION ALL SELECT org_id FROM email_log",

mutations.name: the cutoff is inclusive
mutations._why: `<`, not `<=`. Not about the single row that lands exactly on the boundary so much as the shape: a retention window stated as "90 days" should keep the row at exactly 90 days old. Scored against the probe's whole-day ages, where a row sits on the boundary by construction.
mutations.old: "DELETE FROM stream_access_logs WHERE org_id = $1 AND accessed_at < $2",
mutations.new: "DELETE FROM stream_access_logs WHERE org_id = $1 AND accessed_at <= $2",
mutations.equivalent: A row exactly on the cutoff to the microsecond cannot be arranged from a fixture written in whole days — the ages are relative to now() and every row is milliseconds off the boundary. Kept in the spec as a record of the comparison being deliberate; the boundary itself is pinned by the fixture's 45-and-200-day rows sitting either side of each tier.

mutations.name: the summary under-reports the sweep
mutations._why: The total is what the log line shows an operator. Leaving a table out of the sum under-reports a nightly sweep that deleted hundreds of thousands of rows, and there is nothing else to notice it by.

mutations.name: a merely slow run is reaped
mutations._why: 20 minutes, and a run at 5 is working rather than lost. Reaping it stamps `error` over a run the agent is still in the middle of, and the agent's own /complete then lands on a row that already has a terminal outcome.

mutations.name: a run with no started_at is reaped
mutations._why: `/start` sets `outcome` and `started_at` together, so a `running` row with a NULL `started_at` should not exist — and must not be reaped on the strength of a NULL comparison. Unlike the sweep's equivalent filter this one IS load-bearing, because the NULL is on the column being compared: `NULL < cutoff` excludes it either way, but dropping the predicate here also drops it from the log line's id list.
mutations.old: WHERE outcome = 'running' AND started_at IS NOT NULL AND started_at < $1
mutations.equivalent: Same three-valued logic as the sweep's: `NULL < cutoff` is NULL and WHERE treats that as not-true, so the predicate changes no row. Verified on the fixture's `loops-run-nostart`. Kept so the next reader does not take its presence for evidence it is load-bearing.

mutations.name: the write forgets to re-check running
mutations._why: The re-check belongs in the WRITE, not just the SELECT. Without it a concurrent /complete landing between the two has its real outcome overwritten with `error`, leaving a row carrying `error` beside the completion's own severity and incident_id — and no repair path, because the agent's POST already succeeded.
mutations.equivalent: Unreachable from a probe: it needs a /complete to land between the SELECT and the UPDATE, which a single-threaded probe cannot arrange. Kept as the record of why the predicate is in the write statement at all.

mutations.name: abandoned and stale-pending share a cutoff
mutations._why: Two minutes re-fires the wakeup; six HOURS gives up. Sharing the shorter cutoff abandons a run two minutes after it was queued, which on a cold-starting agent is every run.

mutations.name: a terminal run is abandoned
mutations._why: The abandoned sweep is scoped to `pending`. Without that it stamps every old row including the ones that finished — the fixture's `incident` run is nine hours old and must keep its outcome.

mutations.name: an open cooldown window is drained early
mutations._why: An anchor younger than its org's cooldown is a window still open: draining it emits a digest for a window that has not finished and re-arms the camera for immediate emails, which is the double-email the digest exists to prevent.

mutations.name: the digest counts the event at the anchor
mutations._why: Strictly AFTER the anchor: the immediate email already covered the event at anchor time, so counting it reports one more than actually went unreported. The fixture places an event exactly on the anchor for this.
mutations.old: WHERE org_id = $1 AND camera_id = $2 AND timestamp > $3 AND timestamp <= $4
mutations.new: WHERE org_id = $1 AND camera_id = $2 AND timestamp >= $3 AND timestamp <= $4

mutations.name: the digest counts past the window edge
mutations._why: Events past `window_end` belong to a later cycle. The upper bound is defensive — no later cycle exists yet, because this anchor is still here — but dropping it folds a future cycle's events into this digest.

mutations.name: the anchor is deleted unconditionally
mutations._why: The whole subtlety of this body. Counting and emitting take real time; a motion event landing in that gap sees the same expired anchor, sends its own immediate email and re-arms the row. An unconditional delete erases that brand-new window, so the NEXT event emails immediately again — double immediate emails on exactly the busy cameras digests exist for.
mutations.equivalent: Needs a motion event to land between the count and the delete, which a probe cannot arrange. Kept as the record of why the delete is conditional; the re-armed case is what `anchors_rearmed` in the summary counts.

mutations.name: a corrupt anchor is kept
mutations._why: An unparseable timestamp is dropped so the next motion event starts a fresh window. Keeping it silences that camera FOREVER — every tick re-reads a value nothing can parse, and the immediate-email path sees an anchor and stays quiet.

mutations.name: the digest reads the wrong org's cooldown
mutations._why: The cooldown is the ANCHOR's org's, and the fixture gives one org a two-hour window so a 40-minute anchor is open for it and expired for the other. A port reading a constant flips exactly that row.

mutations.name: an unreachable service is not recorded
mutations._why: A failed check-in still writes `last_check_at` and `last_check_reachable`. Skipping those writes leaves the previous verdict in place with no record that anything was attempted — the one state the grace window cannot reason about, because it cannot tell a stale success from a fresh one.

mutations.name: a non-object body is accepted
mutations._why: A body that parses as JSON but is not an object is not an answer. Accepting one reads `valid` off a list as absent — falsy — so it fails closed by accident rather than by decision, and `reachable` is recorded as true when nothing usable came back.

mutations.name: sync survives an invalid licence
mutations._why: Sync is a separate entitlement but not an independent one: a licence losing validity loses sync in the same breath rather than coasting on a stale `true`. The fixture has a body claiming sync on an invalid licence for exactly this.

mutations.name: an invalid licence still stamps last_ok_at
mutations._why: `last_ok_at` is what the 72-hour grace measures from. Stamping it on a REVOKED check-in means a revoked licence coasts for three more days every time it checks in — which is unbounded, since it checks in every fifteen minutes.

mutations.name: the install id is minted fresh each time
mutations._why: Persisted so it survives a restart: the licence service counts installs, and an id that changed every boot would read as an install per restart — which for a per-install licence means it stops validating. Scored zero because the probe recorded only whether an id EXISTED, which is true either way. It records stability across scenarios now — the same id as the previous check-in — which is the actual behaviour: minted once, then reused.

mutations.name: an unreachable Clerk downgrades the org
mutations._why: The most expensive mistake this sweep could make, and the one it exists because of: treating a missing answer as an answer. `live is None` is a SKIP. Downgrading on it means a Clerk outage moves every paying org to free caps.

mutations.name: the reconcile skips the camera cap
mutations._why: Writing the setting without enforcing the cap looks entirely right in `settings` and leaves the org streaming past its new plan — three cameras over, in the fixture.

mutations.name: the reconcile checks free orgs too
mutations._why: Only PAID cached slugs are re-verified. Widening it to every org means a Clerk lookup per org per hour — the throttle the fast path exists to avoid — and the fixture's free org is there to show it is not touched.
mutations.old: "SELECT org_id, value FROM settings WHERE key = 'org_plan' AND value = ANY($1)",
mutations.new: "SELECT org_id, value FROM settings WHERE key = 'org_plan'",

mutations.name: the cap runs before the plan is written
mutations._why: `enforce_camera_cap` reads the plan back, so running it first applies the cap the org is LEAVING rather than the one it is arriving at — and on a downgrade that means no cameras are suspended at all.

mutations.name: the api key hash is mirrored
mutations._why: The hash that authenticates a node to THIS Command Center. Useless to a restore — a restored node re-registers and is issued a fresh key — and actively dangerous sitting in a cloud mirror. Only observable in the request body, which is why the fake records it.

mutations.name: evidence blobs are mirrored
mutations._why: Tens of megabytes a row, deliberately not synced. The metadata around it still is, so a restore knows the evidence existed. Sending it would also defeat the column's deferral on the Python side.

mutations.name: a log table reconciles deletes
mutations._why: The dangerous direction. `known_ids` lets the service tombstone what is gone locally — right for cameras, catastrophic for a log table, because local retention prunes those BECAUSE local disk is finite and the cloud copy exists to outlive it. Every nightly cleanup would delete the mirror's history too.

mutations.name: the cursor advances on an unacknowledged push
mutations._why: The cursor moves only past rows the service CONFIRMED. Advancing on a 5xx means those rows are never sent again and are silently missing from the mirror — the failure mode a backup can least afford, because nothing surfaces it until a restore.

mutations.name: one table's failure stops the cycle
mutations._why: Cursors are independent, so partial progress is both safe and useful. Aborting the cycle on the first failure means a single persistently failing table blocks every table after it in the list — forever, since the order is fixed.

mutations.name: sync runs without the entitlement
mutations._why: A separate opt-in on the licence. Running without it mirrors a customer's data to a service they did not buy.
mutations.equivalent: The fixture seeds the entitlement ON, so removing the gate changes nothing there — the OFF case is what `is_sync_enabled`'s own tests cover. Kept as the record of the gate being deliberate.

mutations.name: a recovered disk keeps its debounce
mutations._why: Falling back below the threshold CLEARS the debounce, so the next crossing alerts immediately rather than waiting out a six-hour cooldown from an incident that is already over. Unreachable from a differential — there is no HTTP surface — which is why the decision is a function taking its inputs.
mutations._unit_only: The disk check writes nothing and has no route. An earlier version of this note claimed `check_disk_critical`'s own tests already held it; they did not exist, and the mutation scored zero. Second time I made that claim without checking it in this slice. Four tests written: the recovery clearing the debounce, the six-hour cooldown, a zero total not reading as a full disk, and the rounded percentage.
